story.title: Trump Plans Supreme Court Appeal After Court Halts White House Ballroom Construction
story.summary: A federal appeals court has blocked President Trump's $400 million ballroom construction project at the White House, ruling that he cannot proceed without congressional approval. The court's decision affirms a lower court ruling and allows only below-ground construction to continue. Trump has announced his intention to appeal the ruling to the Supreme Court, calling it unjust.

explore_lenses.label: What construction is halted, and what may continue?
explore_lenses.title: Above-ground work is blocked for now
explore_lenses.summary: The ruling preserves the lower court’s bar on the ballroom itself, while distinguishing it from security-related work below ground. Its immediate effect is tempered by a 14-day stay.

claims.text: The D.C. Circuit upheld the preliminary injunction against above-ground ballroom construction; the National Trust said the injunction will bar that work unless Congress acts.
The injunction had allowed work on an underground bunker and other national-security facilities to continue, rather than authorizing the above-ground ballroom.
The appeals ruling is stayed for 14 days, so the timing and scope of any work during that temporary period depend on the stay’s legal effect and any further court order.

explore_lenses.label: Why is private funding not enough, according to the court?
explore_lenses.title: The dispute is over authorization, not just cost
explore_lenses.summary: Trump has argued that privately raised money lets him proceed; the preservation group and lower court have treated congressional authorization for a major change to the White House as the key legal requirement.

claims.text: Trump has said the ballroom’s construction costs would be covered by private donors, and the White House’s original 2025 announcement described the project as privately funded while assigning security enhancements to the Secret Service.

The lower court concluded that no statute authorized demolishing an entire White House wing and replacing it with a privately funded ballroom; it also concluded that the National Park Service lacked relevant statutory authority if it directed or funded the work.

The National Trust’s president, Brent Leggs, said the group’s position is that only Congress can authorize a White House ballroom; Trump has called the ruling politically motivated and argued that the broader complex is needed for national security.

A prior D.C. Circuit order included a dissent by Judge Neomi Rao, who said the government was likely to prevail because the project was authorized as a White House ‘improvement’ and because halting it would prolong security vulnerabilities.

explore_lenses.label: What happens before a Supreme Court appeal?
explore_lenses.title: A temporary stay precedes any high-court action
explore_lenses.summary: Trump has said he will seek Supreme Court review, but the appellate ruling includes a short stay that creates an immediate procedural deadline. A Supreme Court appeal would require a filed application or petition and could also involve a request to keep the injunction paused.

story_report.summary: A federal appeals court has upheld a preliminary injunction blocking above-ground construction of President Donald Trump’s proposed White House ballroom, concluding that congressional approval is required. The ruling leaves the project’s below-ground national-security work unaffected under the earlier injunction, but the appeals decision is stayed for 14 days. Trump said he will ask the Supreme Court to reverse the block, placing the project’s immediate future on whether the administration wins further relief before the injunction takes effect.

sections.heading: Ballroom Funding and Legal Authority
sections.body: Trump has said private donors would cover the ballroom’s construction costs, while the White House’s 2025 announcement described the project as privately funded and assigned security enhancements to the Secret Service. The lower court found no statute authorizing the demolition of an entire White House wing and its replacement with a privately funded ballroom. It also concluded that the National Park Service lacked the relevant statutory authority if it directed or funded the work.

sections.heading: White House Ballroom Security Dispute
sections.body: The National Trust’s president, Brent Leggs, has said that Congress alone can authorize a White House ballroom. Trump has called the ruling politically motivated and maintained that the broader complex is needed for national security. In an earlier D.C. Circuit order, Judge Neomi Rao dissented, saying the government was likely to prevail because the project qualified as a White House improvement and because stopping it would prolong security vulnerabilities.

sections.heading: Supreme Court Appeal Timeline
sections.body: Trump’s announced appeal raises the prospect of Supreme Court review of the merits and potentially a request for emergency relief during the 14-day stay. The immediate legal question is whether the administration secures further court action before the injunction becomes operative. The available reporting as of Aug. 7 did not identify a filed Supreme Court docket entry or establish whether the justices would intervene.

related_stories.title: Senate Approves Bipartisan Sanctions Bill Targeting Russia and Iran
related_stories.summary: The Senate has passed a bipartisan bill imposing stricter sanctions on Russia and extending existing sanctions on Iran. The legislation, which received an overwhelming vote of 86-11, was championed by the late Senator Lindsey Graham, whose recent death expedited its passage. The bill aims to penalize countries that continue to purchase Russian oil and gas, aiming to reduce revenue for Russia amid ongoing conflicts.

related_stories.title: Sen. Cassidy Supports Todd Blanche's Attorney General Confirmation
related_stories.summary: Republican Senator Bill Cassidy has announced his support for Todd Blanche's nomination as attorney general, which is expected to facilitate Blanche's confirmation by the Senate. Cassidy's backing comes after two other Republican senators expressed their opposition to Blanche's nomination, making Cassidy's support crucial for moving forward.

related_stories.title: Trump Resumes Efforts to Dismiss Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook
related_stories.summary: Donald Trump is renewing his attempts to fire Federal Reserve governor Lisa Cook after the US Supreme Court previously blocked his efforts. The administration is moving forward with the dismissal despite Cook's denial of mortgage fraud allegations that prompted the initial attempt to terminate her position.
